subject: governing code (VBBL 2025)
claim: VBBL is the building code in the City of Vancouver. BC Codes do not apply there. VBBL 2025 took effect 15 Sep 2025, replaced VBBL 2019, and aligns with BCBC 2024.
value: `if site.municipality == "Vancouver": code_basis == "VBBL2025"`
source: City of Vancouver, Guide to 2025 VBBL Updates v1.01 (23 Jan 2026), pp. 1–2; BC Gov "2024 BC Codes" page
applicable_limits: Applies to new permit applications from 15 Sep 2025. In-stream applications may stay under VBBL 2019 until 8 Mar 2027. Other Metro Vancouver municipalities use BCBC 2024.

subject: Part 9 scope
claim: Part 9 applies to buildings of ≤3 storeys and ≤600 m² building area with major occupancy C, D, E, F2 or F3. Other buildings fall under Parts 3/4/5.
value: `part9 = storeys <= 3 && building_area_m2 <= 600 && occupancy in {C,D,E,F2,F3}`
applicable_limits: Excludes buildings designed under Div. B 3.2.10. Parts 11–13 cover existing buildings, float homes and temporary uses.

subject: cladding compliance route
claim: Lumber, shingles/shakes, fibre-cement, plywood, OSB, hardboard, vinyl, insulated vinyl, polypropylene, aluminium or steel cladding on wood-frame (or above-ground flat ICF) walls must follow 9.27.2–9.27.13 or Part 5. Stucco, masonry, asphalt shingles and EIFS have their own routes. Any other cladding material, or a listed material on an unlisted substrate, must follow Part 5.
value: `if cladding.material not in PART9_LISTED or substrate not in PART9_SUBSTRATES: route = "Part5"`
applicable_limits: Applies only to walls exposed to precipitation. Unlisted claddings such as terracotta, rammed earth, timber boards on a mass-timber substrate, or cladding on concrete go to Part 5, which needs professional design.

subject: two planes of protection
claim: Walls exposed to precipitation that enclose residential occupancy, or spaces directly serving it, need a first plane (cladding) and a second plane of protection.
value: `if wall.exposed && wall.encloses_residential: has_first_plane && has_second_plane`
applicable_limits: Part 9 only. The Note calls this a "basic rainscreen" and recommends it in all cases.

subject: capillary break (trigger)
claim: A second plane with a capillary break is required when HDD < 3400 and MI > 0.90, or when HDD ≥ 3400 and MI > 1.00.
value: `requires_cap_break = (hdd < 3400 && mi > 0.90) || (hdd >= 3400 && mi > 1.00)`. For Vancouver (HDD 2825/2925, MI 1.4) this is always true.
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.27.2.2.(5) (pdf p. 195); climate inputs from req.vancouver-climate-data
applicable_limits: Part 9, walls exposed to precipitation. See the exceptions entry.

subject: capillary break (exceptions)
claim: The capillary break may be omitted when: it is shown that this won't harm performance; the building is an accessory building; or the wall and the floors it supports or meets are all non-moisture-sensitive, or it is a sufficiently thick mass wall.
value: not machine-checkable (except `building.is_accessory`)
applicable_limits: The 2009 City bulletin confirms detached garages and sheds are exempt. The two planes required by 9.27.2.2.(4) still apply to residential walls.

subject: capillary break (configuration)
claim: A capillary break exists when any one of these holds: (a) a drained and vented air space ≥9.5 mm deep over the full wall; (b) open drainage material ≥10 mm thick and ≥80% open over the full wall; (c) loosely fastened cladding with a continuous clear space ≥10 mm deep at the bottom and ≥6 mm deep over ≥90 mm of every 230 mm of exposed height; (d) masonry cavity wall or veneer to 9.20; (e) EIFS to 9.27.14.
value: `(cavity_depth_mm >= 9.5 && cavity_drained && cavity_vented && full_wall) || (drain_mat_thk_mm >= 10 && drain_mat_open_pct >= 80) || ...`
applicable_limits: Part 9. Part 5 buildings are designed by a professional (see req.part5-rainscreen-note).

subject: rainscreen cavity
claim: The cavity may be interrupted only by openings/services, flashing, and furring covering ≤20% of the furred area. Where a construction projects over the top of the cavity, the cavity must not connect to concealed spaces in the projection (for example a soffit).
value: `furring_area_fraction <= 0.20`; `!cavity_top.connects_to_concealed_space`
applicable_limits: Part 9.

subject: cladding clearance to grade
claim: Cladding that is adversely affected by moisture (examples given: untreated wood, plywood, OSB, waferboard, hardboard) must be at least 200 mm above finished ground.
value: `if cladding.moisture_sensitive: cladding_bottom_above_finished_ground_mm >= 200`
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.27.2.4.(1) (pdf p. 195). The same text appears in VBBL 2019 9.27.2.4.(1).
applicable_limits: Part 9. The code does not say whether treated wood or non-moisture-sensitive claddings (metal, fibre cement) may be lower; see U4. It does not define how to measure from hard landscaping versus soil; see Gaps.

subject: cladding clearance to roof
claim: Moisture-sensitive cladding must be at least 50 mm above a roof surface.
value: `if cladding.moisture_sensitive && below_is_roof: clearance_mm >= 50`
applicable_limits: Applies to roof/deck interfaces only, not grade.

subject: stucco clearance to grade
claim: Stucco must be at least 200 mm above finished ground, unless it is applied over concrete or masonry.
value: `if cladding == "stucco" && substrate not in {concrete, masonry}: stucco_bottom_above_finished_ground_mm >= 200`
applicable_limits: Part 9 stucco only. Parging or render on a concrete plinth is exempt from this clearance.

subject: foundation wall above grade
claim: Exterior foundation walls must extend at least 150 mm above finished ground.
value: `foundation_top_above_finished_ground_mm >= 150`
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.15.4.6.(1). VBBL 2019 has the same.
applicable_limits: Part 9 foundations within the scope of 9.15.1.1. Engineered (Part 4) foundations are not bound by this sentence.

subject: structural wood treatment
claim: Structural wood must be preservative-treated if it is less than 150 mm above finished ground. It must also be treated if it is exposed to precipitation, in a moisture-trapping configuration, and MI > 1.00.
value: `if structural_wood.clearance_to_ground_mm < 150: treated == true`; `if exposed && traps_moisture && mi > 1.00: treated == true` (Vancouver MI 1.4)
applicable_limits: Structural wood elements only; not cladding. Retaining walls and termite clauses are separate.

subject: wood treatment use category
claim: Treatment must follow CSA O80.1 Table 2 use categories. UC4.1 applies to ground contact, or to wood less than 150 mm above ground with no moisture barrier from a permeable support. UC3.2 applies to exterior, above-ground wood that is uncoated or in a moisture-trapping configuration. UC4.2 applies to critical structural parts such as permanent wood foundations.
value: `uc = ground_contact || (clear_mm < 150 && !moisture_barrier) ? "UC4.1" : exterior_above_ground && (uncoated || traps_moisture) ? "UC3.2" : ...`
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.3.2.9.(5) (pdf p. 10–11), citing CAN/CSA-O80.1
applicable_limits: Applies only where 9.3.2.9 requires treatment. The CSA O80 text itself was not read (paywalled).

subject: boron-treated wood
claim: Wood treated to UC1/UC2 with inorganic boron must be kept from direct water exposure during and after construction. If it is less than 150 mm from the ground, it must also be separated from permeable supports by a durable moisture barrier.
value: `if treatment == "boron": !exposed_to_water && (clear_mm >= 150 || moisture_barrier)`
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.3.2.9.(6). Text read in the VBBL 2019 edition; the 2025 sentence exists but was only partly captured.
applicable_limits: Interior/sheltered borate-treated members only.

subject: wood-on-concrete separation
claim: Untreated wood framing supported on concrete that is in contact with ground or fill must be separated from it by ≥0.05 mm polyethylene or Type S roll roofing. This is not required if the wood is at least 150 mm above ground.
value: `if !wood.pressure_treated && support.concrete_in_ground_contact && wood_above_ground_mm < 150: separator in {"PE>=0.05mm","TypeS_roll_roofing"}`
applicable_limits: Part 9 wood-frame. This is a minimum damp-proof separation, not a full DPC specification. Sill-plate sealing is required separately by 9.23.7.2 and 9.25.3.

subject: wood member ends in concrete
claim: Ends of joists or beams framing into concrete or masonry must be treated, or have a 12 mm air space at their ends and sides, where the bottom of the member is at or below ground level. Insulation or membranes must not block this air space.
value: `if member.bottom_at_or_below_grade: member.treated || end_air_space_mm >= 12`
applicable_limits: Applies only to members pocketed into masonry or concrete.

subject: flashing (locations)
claim: Flashing is required at every horizontal junction between cladding elements, every horizontal offset, and every horizontal change of substrate where stresses concentrate or where drainage from above could be compromised. It is not required where: the upper cladding laps the lower by ≥25 mm; both claddings sit outboard of a drained and vented cavity and the joint limits ingress; or at stucco joints with expansion strips over a drained cavity.
value: `for joint in horizontal_cladding_joints: joint.flashed || joint.overlap_mm >= 25 || (joint.both_over_vented_cavity && joint.ingress_minimised)`
applicable_limits: Part 9.

subject: flashing over openings / overhang
claim: Flashing is required over an opening when the vertical distance from the underside of the eave to the top of the trim exceeds one-quarter of the eave's horizontal overhang.
value: `flashing_required = eave_to_trim_top_mm > 0.25 * eave_overhang_mm`
applicable_limits: This is the only code link between overhang depth and wall protection. There is no minimum overhang.

subject: flashing (geometry)
claim: Flashing under 9.27.3.8.(1) and (3) must: rise ≥50 mm behind the sheathing membrane; slope ≥6% outward after frame shrinkage; have end dams ≥25 mm high or ≥ DRWP/10 (Pa) if greater, extending to the cladding face; lap ≥10 mm over the element below; and end in a drip ≥5 mm out from the face below.
value: `upstand_mm >= 50 && slope_pct >= 6 && end_dam_mm >= max(25, drwp_pa/10) && lap_mm >= 10 && drip_offset_mm >= 5`. Vancouver DRWP is 160 Pa, so end_dam_mm >= 25.
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.27.3.8.(4) (pdf p. 197–198); DRWP from req.vancouver-climate-data
applicable_limits: Part 9 wall flashing. Masonry flashings are in 9.20.13.

subject: flashing (material thickness)
claim: Minimum flashing thicknesses: lead 1.73 mm, galvanized steel 0.33 mm, copper 0.46 mm, zinc 0.46 mm, aluminium 0.48 mm, vinyl 1.02 mm.
value: `flashing.thickness_mm >= MIN[flashing.material]`
applicable_limits: Part 9. With stucco, aluminium flashing needs an impervious separation (9.28.1.5).

subject: sill flashing
claim: Sills of windows and doors that are not self-flashing need flashing between the sill underside and the wall below.
value: `if !opening.self_flashing: sill_flashing == true`
applicable_limits: Part 9.

subject: sheathing membrane
claim: At least one layer of sheathing membrane meeting CAN/CGSB-51.32-M is required behind cladding, with laps ≥100 mm and upper sheets over lower ones. Exceptions exist for insulating sheathing and face-sealed panels.
value: `membrane_layers >= 1 && lap_mm >= 100 && shingle_lapped`
applicable_limits: Part 9. The "face sealed" exception 9.27.3.6 does not remove the capillary break required by 9.27.2.2.(5).

subject: furring
claim: Furring for cladding over sheathing must be ≥19 × 38 mm lumber, fastened to the framing, at ≤600 mm o.c.
value: `furring.thk_mm >= 19 && furring.width_mm >= 38 && furring.spacing_mm <= 600`
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.27.5.3. Read in the VBBL 2019 edition; the 2025 article exists (referenced from 9.27.2.2.(1)(a)) but its text was not separately captured.
applicable_limits: Part 9.

subject: cladding fasteners
claim: Cladding fasteners must be corrosion-resistant and compatible with the cladding. Wood cladding fasteners must penetrate ≥25 mm into framing or through the nail base (≥19 mm for shakes and shingles).
value: `fastener.corrosion_resistant && penetration_mm >= 25`
source: VBBL 2019 9.27.5.5, 9.27.5.7 (2025 text not separately captured)
applicable_limits: Part 9.

subject: sealant at cladding change
claim: Vertical joints between different cladding materials must be sealed, unless they are lapped or flashed against rain.
value: `if joint.vertical && materials_differ: sealed || lapped || flashed`
applicable_limits: Part 9.

subject: masonry veneer base
claim: Masonry veneer on wood frame needs a ≥25 mm air space behind it. Weep holes are required at ≤800 mm spacing at the bottom of the cavity. Base flashing must run from ≥5 mm beyond the face below to 150 mm up the frame wall, behind the membrane or insulating sheathing.
value: `airspace_mm >= 25 && weep_spacing_mm <= 800 && flashing_projection_mm >= 5 && flashing_upstand_mm >= 150`
applicable_limits: Part 9 masonry veneer only.

subject: foundation damp-proofing
claim: Where outside finished ground is higher than the inside ground level, foundation walls must be damp-proofed below ground, from finished ground level down to the top of the footing. Materials must be ASTM/CGSB/CSA listed, or ≤43 ng/(Pa·s·m²) of the listed types.
value: `if exterior_grade > interior_grade: dampproof.from == "finished_ground" && dampproof.to == "top_of_footing"`
applicable_limits: Applies only where 9.14 drainage is provided. Hydrostatic conditions need waterproofing (9.13.3). Soil gas (9.13.4) is not covered here.

subject: foundation drainage
claim: Unless shown unnecessary, the bottom of every exterior foundation wall must be drained by tile or pipe (≥100 mm diameter, ≥150 mm granular cover) or by a granular layer (≥125 mm deep, extending ≥300 mm beyond the footing). Drains must go to a sewer, ditch or dry well (dry well ≥5 m from the building).
value: `drain_pipe_dia_mm >= 100 && pipe_cover_mm >= 150` or `granular_depth_mm >= 125 && granular_extension_mm >= 300`
applicable_limits: Part 9. Book II (Plumbing) Art. 2.4.2.5 also governs foundation drain connection; not read.

subject: surface grading
claim: The building must be located, or the site graded, so that water does not accumulate at or near the building. No slope value is given.
value: not machine-checkable as written. A proxy is `grade_slope_away_from_wall > 0`, but the threshold is not code.
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.14.6.1.(1); Part 5 equivalent VBBL25-V1 5.7.1.2.(1)
applicable_limits: Performance requirement only.

subject: downspout discharge
claim: Downspouts not connected to a sewer need extensions that carry rainwater away from the building without causing soil erosion.
value: `if downspout && !connected_to_sewer: has_extension && discharges_away_from_wall`
source: VBBL25-V2, 9.26.18.2.(1); Part 5 equivalent VBBL25-V1, 5.6.2.2.(3)
applicable_limits: No minimum extension length is given.

subject: Part 5 deflection features
claim: In Part 5 buildings, flashings, drips or overhangs must be used to deflect water off the building face at changes in wall or roof plane, changes in cladding material, and window or door heads or sills.
value: `for each (plane_change | cladding_change | opening_head | opening_sill): has_flashing || has_drip || has_overhang`
applicable_limits: Part 5 (buildings outside Part 9, or Part 9 claddings routed to Part 5).

subject: Part 5 rainscreen
claim: A Vancouver explanatory note treats rainscreen as the minimum for vertical envelope assemblies in Part 5 buildings. Cladding over light wood or steel framing goes over a drained cavity with through-wall flashings. The note recommends a cavity of at least 19 mm, or at least 12 mm where a full exterior membrane is used and all insulation is outboard. Exposed columns, beams and walkways may be exempt only if built of preservative-treated or durable materials.
value: `cavity_depth_mm >= 19` (recommended), `>= 12` (exterior-insulated case)
source: VBBL25-V1, Note A-5.6.1.2 "Protective Material" (printed p. 691–692)
applicable_limits: Notes are explanatory and not mandatory requirements. Applies to Part 5 design by a building envelope professional.

subject: Part 5 surface water
claim: Part 5: site grading, building location or redirection must prevent surface water from accumulating against the building. Drainage must direct water away from assemblies that separate interior space from the ground, unless they are designed for hydrostatic pressure.
value: not machine-checkable
applicable_limits: Part 5. Below-grade waterproofing/damp-proofing is in 5.7.2–5.7.3.

subject: concrete (plinth) strength
claim: Unreinforced concrete must meet CSA A23.1 "R" class. Minimum 28-day strength: 15 MPa for walls and footings; 32 MPa (or 30 MPa where local aggregate can't reach 32) for exterior steps and garage floors. Site-batched concrete for those uses needs 5–8% air. Maximum w/cm: 0.70 for walls and footings, 0.45 for exterior steps.
value: `if element in {exterior_step, garage_floor}: fc_mpa >= 32 (or 30) && wcm <= 0.45`; `if element in {foundation_wall, footing}: fc_mpa >= 15 && wcm <= 0.70`
applicable_limits: Part 9 unreinforced or nominally reinforced concrete only. Reinforced concrete goes to Part 4 and CSA A23.1/A23.3 exposure classes (not verified, U7).

subject: guard at raised surface
claim: A guard is required on any accessible walking surface (including exterior landings, porches and raised walkways) that is more than 600 mm above the adjacent surface within 1.2 m.
value: `if surface.walkable && drop_within_1200mm_mm > 600: has_guard`
applicable_limits: Part 9. Applies to walkable surfaces, not seats as such. Maintenance-only access is exempt.

subject: exterior seat
claim: No VBBL provision governs the height or form of an exterior façade seat. The seat provisions found cover fixed seats in places of assembly (3.3.2) and the bench in accessible showers (3.8.3.17, 480–520 mm high), which do not apply to this edge.
value: not applicable
source: VBBL25-V1, Div. B 3.3.2.4, 3.3.2.8, 3.8.3.17 (searched full text for "bench")
applicable_limits: Search covered Volume 1 (Parts 3–8) and Volume 2 (Part 9). It did not cover street/landscape design guidelines, which may have bench standards.

subject: Vancouver design climate
claim: Vancouver design climate data. City Hall: HDD 2825, MI 1.4, DRWP (1-in-5) 160 Pa, annual rain 1325 mm, annual total precipitation 1400 mm, 15-min rain 10 mm, 1-day rain (1/50) 112 mm. Granville & 41st: HDD 2925, otherwise similar. Future 2020s HDD 2471; 2050s HDD 2102 (no MI or DRWP given).
value: inputs: `hdd = 2825; mi = 1.4; drwp_pa = 160`
source: VBBL25-V1, Div. B Appendix C, Table C-2 (pdf p. 934, printed p. 146)
applicable_limits: Two in-city locations plus future projections. No exposure or orientation classification.

subject: rainscreen (City bulletin)
claim: City bulletin for one- and two-family dwellings. All new dwellings need rainscreen (exceptions: vinyl or aluminium siding, mass walls). Cavity ≥10 mm, ≥80% open, vented, with insect screens. Flashing above and below openings and at cladding changes, with 25 mm end dams. Permits need wall details for each cladding plus a transition detail. Inspections include a rainscreen inspection before cladding.
value: `cavity_depth_mm >= 10 && cavity_open_pct >= 80 && vents_screened`
source: City of Vancouver Bulletin 2009-009-BU (29 Apr 2009), "Rainscreen Design and Inspection for One and Two Family Dwellings"
applicable_limits: Pre-dates VBBL 2019 and 2025. Where it conflicts with VBBL 2025 text, the By-law governs. Detached garages and sheds are exempt.

subject: bioreceptivity (concept)
claim: bioreceptivity (definition)
value: Defined as a material's ability or potential to be colonised by living organisms (Guillitte 1995). Guillitte gave six types (primary, secondary, tertiary, intrinsic, extrinsic, semi-extrinsic). The 2021 reanalysis proposes dropping intrinsic, extrinsic and semi-extrinsic and adding "quaternary". [read: abstract]
source: Sanmartín, P., Miller, A.Z., Prieto, B., Viles, H.A. (2021). Revisiting and reanalysing the concept of bioreceptivity 25 years on. *Science of the Total Environment* 770, 145314. doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.145314
applicable_limits: A conceptual definition only. It gives no per-material values. Guillitte's 1995 original was not read.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: building stone (bioreceptivity)
claim: bioreceptivity of stone (review)
value: A review of the bioreceptivity of building stones exists. Its content was not read. [snippet: bibliographic record only]
source: Miller, A.Z., Sanmartín, P., Pereira-Pardo, L., Dionísio, A., Saiz-Jimenez, C., Macedo, M.F., Prieto, B. (2012). Bioreceptivity of building stones: A review. *Science of the Total Environment* 426, 1–12. doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2012.03.026
applicable_limits: Placeholder until read. Do not draw values from this entry.

subject: timber
claim: decay moisture threshold (all timber)
value: Wood is not safe from decay until its MC is below about 20%. Spores germinate poorly below fibre saturation (about 25–30% MC). Decay fungi typically need about 35–50% MC. Optimum growth is about 18–35 °C. Fungi are dormant near freezing but are not killed. [read]
source: Baker, M.C. (1969). CBD-111 Decay of Wood. Canadian Building Digest, Division of Building Research, National Research Council Canada.
applicable_limits: A 1969 digest, read from a mirror copy. Covers decay fungi, not surface mould. Thresholds vary with species and fungus. Fluctuating wetting is not quantified.

subject: timber
claim: decay moisture threshold (cross-check)
value: 20% MC is treated as a safety margin against decay. Kiln-dried (sterile) lumber is unlikely to be infected below about 25% MC. 20–30% is a "grey area". [snippet]
source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory paper (morri02a). Authors and title not confirmed; the file name suggests Morris (2002).
applicable_limits: Not opened. Use as corroboration only.

subject: timber (softwoods, red alder)
claim: UV / weathering erosion (softwoods & red alder)
value: 14-year exposure near Madison, Wisconsin. Erosion ranged from 33 µm/yr (lodgepole pine latewood) to 58 µm/yr (western hemlock and red alder earlywood). [read: abstract]
source: Williams, R.S., Knaebe, M.T., Feist, W.C. (2001). Erosion rates of wood during natural weathering. Part II. Earlywood and latewood erosion rates. *Wood and Fiber Science* 33(1).
applicable_limits: Unfinished wood, vertical exposure, in a continental (Wisconsin) climate, not Vancouver. Earlywood erodes faster than latewood.

subject: timber (softwoods incl. WRC)
claim: UV / weathering erosion (incl. WRC)
value: 16-year study: erosion ranged from 34 µm/yr (southern pine latewood) to 101 µm/yr (western red cedar earlywood). Vertical-grain lumber eroded faster than flat-grain plywood. [snippet]
source: Williams, R.S. et al. (2001). Erosion rates of wood during natural weathering. Part I. Effects of grain angle and surface texture. *Wood and Fiber Science*.
applicable_limits: Abstract seen only in a search summary. Same climate caveat as above.

subject: coated timber cladding (spruce)
claim: thermal (surface heating)
value: Darker coatings on spruce cladding raise board temperature under sun, even on low-sun days. Studied as temperature distribution through the board depth. [snippet]
source: WSE Network page: "Temperature distribution within claddings of different coating colors" (Norwegian spruce study; citation not confirmed).
applicable_limits: Not opened. Spruce, Norway. Relates surface temperature to cracking, not directly to drying rate.

subject: wood-to-ground clearance
claim: splash-zone clearance (code)
value: BCBC 2018 Part 9: dampproofing is not required where the wood member is at least 150 mm above the ground. [snippet]
source: British Columbia Building Code 2018, Division B, Part 9 (9.23).
applicable_limits: Applies to wood framing supported on concrete, not to cladding. Confirm in the current BCBC / Vancouver Building By-law.

subject: rainscreen cladding (Vancouver)
claim: Vancouver cladding context
value: Since May 2007 the Vancouver Building By-law has required two-plane (rainscreen) cladding for one- and two-family dwellings, with a drained, vented cavity of at least 10 mm. [snippet]
source: City of Vancouver (2009). Bulletin 2009-009: Rainscreen design and inspection for one and two family dwellings.
applicable_limits: 2009 bulletin; may be superseded. A context entry, not a material property.

subject: lime render
claim: water absorption / capillary uptake
value: **moderate–high**. Higher lime content means more water absorbed. Higher aggregate content gives faster drying and higher permeability. [snippet]
source: Rendering-mortar laboratory study, *Environmental Earth Sciences* (2014), hosted by Univ. Granada group 179. Authors not confirmed.
applicable_limits: Lab mortars, not aged field renders. The mix ratio controls the result.

subject: lime render
claim: surface texture / porosity
value: **porous**. More open porosity gives more water absorption, higher vapour permeability and lower vapour-diffusion resistance. [snippet]
source: Rendering-mortar study, *Ambiente Construído* (SciELO Brazil). Authors not confirmed.
applicable_limits: General relationship for rendering mortars. No specific lime product.

subject: lime render
claim: vapour permeability (drying)
value: μ ≤ 6 for one lime render product. [snippet]
source: EWI Store. EWI-747 Lime Render 3.5 technical data sheet.
applicable_limits: **Single product.** Μ (vapour resistance factor) differs by product and with additives.
suggestion_reason: snippet only; manufacturer source; calculated but not fully read

subject: lime render
claim: drying rate
value: **fast** compared with cement render. Lime renders are vapour-open and let moisture in the wall escape. A 1:1:6 cement:lime:sand render absorbs more, cracks less and dries faster than sand–cement. [snippet]
source: Back to Earth. "Lime vs cement based renders" (trade article).
applicable_limits: A lime supplier, so likely biased. The comparison is qualitative and has no drying-time numbers.

subject: lime render
claim: bioreceptivity
value: **yes, high relative to cement**. Lime-trass mortars, and to a lesser extent natural hydraulic lime (NHL) mortars, best supported wall-plant growth. Highly porous bricks and mortars were most bioreceptive. Weak (low bond strength) brick–mortar combinations favoured growth. [read: abstract]
source: Lubelli, B., Moerman, J., Esposito, R., Mulder, K. (2021). Influence of brick and mortar properties on bioreceptivity of masonry: Results from experimental research. *Construction and Building Materials* 266, 121036. doi:10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2020.121036
applicable_limits: Lab tests with two vascular wall plants (ivy-leaved toadflax, yellow corydalis), not algae or moss. Masonry mortar, not render coats. Higher bioreceptivity trades off against strength.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: lime render
claim: UV / weathering, maintenance
value: Traditional lime finishes are partly **sacrificial** and were regularly renewed. Salt damage moves to the render face. Recoat with a compatible finish (limewash or oil paint), the same one used before. [snippet]
source: Building Conservation Directory / Historic Churches (2021), p.12; Bradford Council, "Rendering" guidance PDF.
applicable_limits: No interval in years was found (see Gaps). Heritage context.

subject: lime render
claim: application sensitivity
value: Substrate suction must be controlled. Too much or too little suction weakens the bond. [snippet]
source: EWI Store. "What is lime render" (supplier article).
applicable_limits: A workmanship note, not an in-service property.

subject: cement render
claim: water absorption
value: **low** through the face. Dense and highly resistant to vapour transfer. [snippet]
source: Back to Earth, "Lime vs cement based renders"
applicable_limits: Lime-supplier source. Applies to uncracked render.

subject: cement render
claim: drying rate (wall behind)
value: **slow**. The render is brittle and cracks. Water enters through the cracks and is trapped behind the render, which can cause freeze–thaw damage in lime-mortar masonry behind it. [snippet]
source: Back to Earth (as above); RICS isurv, "Refurbishment: breathable renders".
applicable_limits: A qualitative mechanism with no field measurements. Depends on substrate and detailing.

subject: cement render
claim: bioreceptivity
value: **low when fresh, rising with age**. OPC binders have a high pH. Carbonation lowers surface pH and favours colonisation. (Evidence is from OPC mortars; see 2.6.) [snippet]
source: See ev.concrete.bioreceptivity-ph and ev.concrete.carbonation-ph
applicable_limits: Inferred from mortar and concrete studies, not render-specific.

subject: cement render

subject: granite
claim: water absorption

source: Engineering geology lecture notes (Univ. of Lucknow, "Engg properties of rocks"); Stone World, "Granite, limestone and marble, Part I".

applicable_limits: Very variable. The ASTM C616 8% limit was seen only in a secondary table (Scribd).

subject: sandstone
claim: freeze–thaw
value: Over 100 cycles, damage developed mainly in the first 50. Sandstone kept its integrity better than tuff. [snippet]
source: Univ. Miskolc *Geosciences* journal article (2026), sandstone and tuff freeze–thaw (authors not confirmed).

subject: natural stone
claim: bioreceptivity
value: **yes (sandstone, limestone)**. Colonisation follows moisture, light, temperature and nutrients. In coarse sandstone, larger grains mean higher porosity and absorption. Lichens occupy the gaps between grains and fill surface pores. Effects are case-specific. Some lichens cut capillary uptake and thermo-hygric stress (Angkor), while some algal and cyanobacterial biofilms raised uptake. [read]
source: Pinna, D. (2014). Biofilms and lichens on stone monuments: do they damage or protect? *Frontiers in Microbiology* 5, 133. doi:10.3389/fmicb.2014.00133
applicable_limits: Heritage monuments, multiple climates. Granite not covered.

subject: sandstone

source: Czech Geological Survey, *Zprávy o geologických výzkumech* 2017.28 (authors not confirmed).
