source: Pittau, F. et al. (2022). *IOP Conf. Ser.: Earth Environ. Sci.* 1078, 012069.
applicable_limits: Co-authors and title not confirmed.

subject: mycelium composites
claim: service life
value: No outdoor field data found. Composites biodegraded within 30 days in soil (packaging study).
source: Packaging Insights news on a mycology packaging study.
applicable_limits: A packaging context. Indicates unsuitability for ground contact.

subject: cork cladding
claim: water absorption
value: 0.17 kg/m² by partial immersion (MDFacade). Standard boards are described as not absorbing water by capillarity. [snippet]
source: Amorim Cork Insulation. MDFacade application pages (bcork.amorim.com).
applicable_limits: **Single product.** Test standard and duration not stated. The page could not be fetched (DNS failure).

subject: cork cladding
claim: vapour resistance
value: μ = 20. Density about 140 ± 10 kg/m³. λ = 0.043 W/m·K. Euroclass E. [snippet]
source: Amorim (as above)
applicable_limits: As above.

subject: cork cladding
claim: service life
value: Claimed 50–60 years "without loss of characteristics". [snippet]
source: Amorim (as above)
applicable_limits: A marketing claim. UV and colour change not covered.

subject: overhang
claim: RDH monitored Lower Mainland multi-family rainscreen buildings. Driving rain was expressed as % of horizontal (vertical-falling) rain, Jan–Oct 2002, with gauges 4 m below the roofline. Results: east wall 3% with a 500 mm overhang, 10% with a 50 mm overhang; south wall 1% and 4% respectively. A building with no overhang gave 13% (6th floor, 3 m below roof) and 5% (3rd floor, 10 m below roof). The authors conclude that overhangs reduce wetting roughly in proportion to their size and their ratio to wall height. They warn that the sample is very small.
value: `wdr_factor_overhang`: O/H ≈ 0 → 1.0; O/H ≈ 0.0125 (50 mm at 4 m) → ~0.75; O/H ≈ 0.125 (500 mm at 4 m) → ~0.25–0.3, relative to no overhang. Interpolate between these points.
source: Hubbs, B. & Hircock, M. (2003). *Building Envelope Performance Monitoring*. Proc. 9th Canadian Conference on Building Science and Technology (CCBST), Vancouver. RDH Building Engineering. Funded by HPO, BC Housing and CMHC. Table 4 and Fig. 7; conclusions p. 14.
applicable_limits: 3 buildings, 1 season, 2 elevations. Wind-driven-rain gauges were on wall faces of 3–6 storey wood-frame buildings, not at the wall base. Results are confounded by neighbouring buildings and site exposure. The paper says the program was 60% complete. Gives no data for single-storey houses or for splash.

subject: overhang
claim: Field study of a six-storey low-slope-roof building in Vancouver with a **retractable** overhang and 31 wind-driven-rain gauges. Findings: the overhang significantly reduces wind-driven rain, especially directly below it. The larger overhang protects more. Protection increases from the façade's side edges to its centre and from bottom to top. Effectiveness falls roughly linearly with distance below the roofline, more slowly for the larger overhang. It also falls as wind speed rises and improves for oblique winds.
value: `overhang_protection(z)` falls roughly linearly with distance `z` below the eave and is scaled down by wind speed. Wall-base protection is less than wall-top protection.
source: Ge, H., Chiu, V. & Stathopoulos, T. (2017). Effect of overhang on wind-driven rain wetting of facades on a mid-rise building: Field measurements. *Building and Environment* 118, 234–250. doi:10.1016/j.buildenv.2017.03.034
applicable_limits: Only the abstract was read (via a bibliographic record); the effectiveness percentages were not seen. One mid-rise building with a flat roof. The "long rainy winters, mild wind and rain" climate is explicitly the context. Low-rise behaviour may differ.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: overhang
claim: The CMHC-commissioned survey of 46 low-rise wood-frame buildings in the Lower Mainland (37 with failures, 9 without) examined 72 walls. It found a strong inverse relation between overhang depth and the share of walls with problems: reportedly nearly 90% at no overhang versus 25% with about 600 mm. About 90% of problems were at interfaces and penetrations, and exterior rain was the dominant moisture source.
value: `failure_risk_multiplier` falls as overhang depth rises. Default anchors: 0 mm → high; ~600 mm → about 0.3× the no-overhang rate.
source: Morrison Hershfield Ltd. (1996). *Survey of Building Envelope Failures in the Coastal Climate of British Columbia*. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Ottawa. Numbers as reported by Bailes, A. (2022). "Roof Overhangs and Moisture Problems", GreenBuildingAdvisor, 28 Apr 2022.
url: https://www.aivc.org/node/24931 (bibliographic record; the PDF text layer was not machine-readable) ; https://www.greenbuildingadvisor.com/article/roof-overhangs-and-moisture-problems
applicable_limits: The overhang percentages come from a blog reading of the report's chart and were not checked against the original. Covers 1980s–90s face-sealed, mostly stucco, vinyl and wood walls on 3–4 storey condos. Shows correlation, not causation.

subject: overhang
claim: Field measurement and modelling show that overhangs and peaked roofs cut rain deposition by about 50%. A BC damage survey correlated overhang size with the probability of rain damage.
value: `wdr_factor_overhang_default = 0.5` when any overhang plus pitched roof is present on a low-rise building
source: Straube, J. (2011). *BSD-013: Rain Control in Buildings* (rev. 22 Aug 2011). Building Science Corporation.
applicable_limits: A rule of thumb without a stated depth. The original studies are not named in the digest.

subject: overhang
claim: The code requires head flashing over an opening when the vertical distance from the eave underside to the top of the trim exceeds ¼ of the eave's horizontal overhang. In other words, the code treats only the band within O/4 below the eave as fully sheltered.
value: `fully_sheltered = (depth_below_eave ≤ 0.25 × overhang_depth)`. For a wall base this is almost never true. For example, a 600 mm overhang shelters only the top 150 mm.
source: Vancouver Building By-law 2014, Div. B, Sentence 9.27.3.8.(3)
applicable_limits: A prescriptive code threshold for flashing, not a measured wetting function. It is conservative. Check against VBBL 2025 (see 01).

subject: wind-driven rain
claim: Driving rain on a wall is approximately DRF × V(z) × rain rate × cos θ × RDF, and further multiplied by height/exposure and topography factors. DRF is about 0.20–0.25 for average rain, up to 0.5 for drizzle and about 0.15 for cloudbursts. RDF is 1.0 near the upper corners of blunt buildings and much less on most of the façade; the worked example uses 0.5 for a peaked-roof bungalow with a 300 mm overhang. Apply a ×0.5 shelter factor when obstructions of building height are within 2× the building height. The worked example also applies a ×0.7 height factor for a 2.7 m bungalow wall.
value: `wall_rain_mm_h = 0.22 × V10_m_s × rain_mm_h × cos(θ) × RDF × EHF × shelter`. Defaults: RDF = 0.5 for a low-rise pitched roof with overhang; EHF = 0.7 for a 1-storey wall; shelter = 0.5 in suburban/urban infill.
source: Straube, J. (2010). *BSD-148: Simplified Prediction of Driving Rain on Buildings: ASHRAE 160P and WUFI 4.0* (14 Nov 2010). Building Science Corporation.
applicable_limits: The full RDF/EHF tables are in figures that were not read. Free-field accuracy is about 10%. Studies comparing it with full-scale measurements report errors up to a factor of 2–5 at individual façade points for Straube–Burnett- and ISO-type models (search-index summary of Heriot-Watt / TU/e comparison papers; not read directly).
suggestion_reason: no reading marker in file; calculated but not fully read

subject: wind-driven rain
claim: For the worst-exposed part of a low-rise building, deposition is roughly 10–20% of (wind speed × rain intensity) for each orientation. Exposed houses may receive tens to hundreds of L/m² per year, while sheltered single-storey houses with wide overhangs receive much less.
value: Cross-check: annual wall rain on an exposed low-rise façade is about 0.1–0.2 × the annual Σ(V·r) for that orientation
source: Straube 2011, BSD-013 (as above)
applicable_limits: Order-of-magnitude only.

subject: wind-driven rain
claim: On a six-storey building, the 3rd-floor gauge received only 38% of the driving rain at the 6th floor. This is attributed to sheltering by neighbouring buildings and to the general wind pattern that wets the tops of mid- and high-rise buildings most.
value: Wall-base WDR is no more than wall-top WDR. Default `base_vs_top_factor` ≈ 0.4 for multi-storey façades.
source: Hubbs & Hircock 2003 (as above)
applicable_limits: One building, one elevation, one season.

subject: wind-driven rain
claim: Wind-driven rain is the largest moisture source for façades. It concentrates at top edges and vertical edges because raindrops are swept toward them, and roof overhangs shelter the parts below. The review classifies quantification methods as experimental, semi-empirical and numerical.
value: Wetting map: corners and top band > field of wall > sheltered base. Overhang shelter is applied as a separate factor.
source: Blocken, B. & Carmeliet, J. (2004). A review of wind-driven rain research in building science. *J. Wind Eng. Ind. Aerodyn.* 92(13), 1079–1130.
applicable_limits: Only the abstract and search-index summaries were read; the PDF text was not extractable. Mostly concerns building-scale wind-driven rain, not ground splash.

subject: driving rain index
claim: ISO 15927-3 computes an annual-average driving-rain index and a spell index for a wall orientation from hourly wind and rain data. It corrects for terrain roughness, topography, obstructions and wall/building type. It is not valid in mountainous terrain with cliffs or gorges, where more than 25% of rain comes from convective storms, or where snow or hail is significant.
value: If hourly YVR data are later used, compute an orientation-specific index per ISO 15927-3. Until then, use the BSD-148 formula.
source: ISO 15927-3:2009 *Hygrothermal performance of buildings — Calculation and presentation of climatic data — Part 3: Calculation of a driving rain index for vertical surfaces from hourly wind and rain data*. Confirmed 2021.
applicable_limits: Paywalled; only the scope was read. Coefficients were not verified.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: splash zone / cladding clearance
claim: Moisture-sensitive cladding (untreated wood, plywood, OSB, hardboard) must be at least 200 mm above finished ground. Stucco must be at least 200 mm above finished ground unless it is over concrete or masonry. NRC's intent statement for the clearance is to limit splashing, soaking or pooling of precipitation against the lower cladding.
value: `splash_zone_height = 200 mm` above finished grade (code minimum). Cladding below it is flagged `at_risk`.
source: VBBL 2014 Div. B 9.27.2.4.(1) and 9.28.1.4. NRC intent per an archived NBC 2005 Intent Statement (search-index only; see Unverified).
applicable_limits: A code minimum, not a measured splash height. Masonry and concrete bases are exempt.
suggestion_reason: snippet only; calculated but not fully read

subject: splash zone / cladding clearance
claim: Keep siding at least 200 mm (8 in) above grade against splash, and slope grade away from the wall.
value: Same as above; corroborates 200 mm.
source: Straube 2011, BSD-013
applicable_limits: Rule of thumb.

subject: splash zone (plinth)
claim: German façade-system practice, referencing DIN 18533-1 water-exposure class W4-E ("splash water and soil moisture at the wall base"), divides the edge into zones. **Façade:** at least 30 cm above finished ground. **Plinth (Sockel):** from 30 cm above to 20 cm below finished ground. **Perimeter:** more than 20 cm below. The splash zone is the part of the plinth above ground. The guide stresses fixing the final ground level early, for all trades. It lists splash water, shading by planting, algae and fungi, and mechanical impact as plinth loads.
value: `splash_zone = 0–300 mm` above grade, a stricter variant of the code's 200 mm. `buried_transition = 0–200 mm` below grade.
source: Caparol Farben Lacke Bautenschutz GmbH (c. 2022). *Capatect Sockel* (plinth systems brochure, 300730_CAP-25066), pp. 6–8. Cites DIN 18533-1.
applicable_limits: A commercial document for ETICS/render plinths. The DIN text itself was not read. The 300 mm is a zoning convention, not a measured splash height.

subject: ground surface at wall base
claim: No measured study was found on splash height versus ground surface (soil, gravel or paving) at building walls. One case report describes rot of log walls where water splashed back from concrete pavers beside the wall, although the rest of the perimeter was graded away. Practitioner reports say gravel absorbs splash better than bare soil or slabs.
value: Illustrative ordering of `splash_intensity`: hard paving > bare soil > gravel strip ≈ vegetated mulch. Coefficients are to be labelled illustrative.
source: "Down to earth detailing", *The Construction Specifier* (Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates authors), log-cabin case.
applicable_limits: Anecdotal case evidence only (search-index summary; full article not read).

subject: drip edge
claim: A 1.2 × 1.2 m test wall had water run off sill/flashing profiles at 15 L/h. Results: unhemmed 45° kick-out drips (20 ga) shed more than 90% of water within the first 1.2 m below. Hems wick water back to the wall and were the single biggest factor reducing shedding. A 45 mm projection generally beat 20 mm. A sloped stone sill with a 20 mm projection put no water into the collection troughs. The authors call the work preliminary, with variable repeat tests. Without an effective drip, sill runoff concentrates on the wall below and causes staining and deterioration.
value: With a drip of at least 20 mm projection and no hem, the wall below receives ≤ 0.1 × the sill runoff. With no drip, the wall below receives about 1.0 × the runoff, concentrated in a streak.
source: Smegal, J. & Trainor, T. (2015). "The effectiveness of different drip edge designs." *Construction Canada*, 5 Feb 2015 (Building Science Laboratories / RDH).
applicable_limits: Single wall height, high flow, no wind. Window sill flashings, not base-of-wall flashings.

subject: base flashing
claim: Flashing must extend at least 50 mm up behind the sheathing membrane, slope at least 6% outward, have end dams, lap the element below by at least 10 mm vertically, and end in a drip offset at least 5 mm from the face below.
value: Base flashing rule: `drip_offset ≥ 5 mm`, `slope ≥ 6%`. If these are absent, apply "no drip" behaviour.
applicable_limits: Code minimums. See 01 for the VBBL 2025 end-dam height.

subject: capillary break
claim: A capillary break, meaning a drained and vented air space of at least 9.5 mm or an open drainage material of at least 9.5 mm that is at least 80% open, is required where HDD < 3400 and MI > 0.90. Vancouver has MI 1.44 and HDD 2925, so it is required.
value: `rainscreen_required(Vancouver) = true`. `min_cavity = 9.5 mm`.
source: VBBL 2014 Div. B 9.27.2.2.(1) and (5); climate values from VBBL 2014 Table 1.1.3.1.A
applicable_limits: Accessory buildings and some others are exempt (9.27.2.2.(6)).

subject: capillary break
claim: Water can bridge gaps up to about 6 mm by capillarity, so a well-defined airspace is needed. About 10 mm is usually specified for tolerance. Water drains through very small continuous gaps. Gaps of 3 mm allow little ventilation; more than 10 mm is needed for significant ventilation. Hydrophobic membranes can also act as capillary breaks.
value: `capillary_bridge = gap < 6 mm`. `drains = gap > 0 and continuous`. `ventilates = gap ≥ 10 mm`.
source: Straube 2011, BSD-013
applicable_limits: Rule-of-thumb values.

subject: wood-on-concrete separation
claim: Untreated wood framing on concrete that is in contact with the ground must be separated by at least 0.05 mm polyethylene or Type S roll roofing. This is not needed if the wood is at least 150 mm above ground. Members framing into concrete or masonry at or below ground must be treated or have a 12 mm air space at their ends and sides.
value: `sill_dpc_required = (wood_untreated && bears_on_concrete && height_above_ground < 150 mm)`. Missing DPC leads to sill wicking and decay risk.
applicable_limits: Code minimum. Ground-contact preservation (9.3.2.9) is covered in 01.

subject: foundation drain
claim: The foundation drain tile must be at least 100 mm in diameter and laid on undisturbed or compacted soil. Its top and sides are covered with at least 150 mm of coarse clean granular material with no more than 10% passing a 4 mm sieve. Alternatively, a granular drainage layer at least 125 mm deep under the footings, extending 300 mm beyond them, drains to a sump. The site must be graded so water does not accumulate at or near the building.
value: `drain_gravel_clean = fines ≤ 10%`. Ageing rule: fines fraction rises over time (see silting gap) and drainage capacity falls (illustrative).
applicable_limits: Below-grade drainage only. The code sets no slope value and has no clause on surface gravel strips.

subject: backfill / grading
claim: Backfill must be placed without damaging the wall, drain, insulation or damp-proofing. It must be graded so that after settling it does not drain toward the foundation. Within 600 mm of the wall it must be free of debris and of boulders larger than 250 mm.
value: Ageing: `grade_settlement` over the first few years can reverse the slope (illustrative timing). Initial slope must be away from the wall.
applicable_limits: Settlement magnitude and timing are not specified.

subject: foundation damp-proofing
claim: Where exterior grade is above interior grade, below-grade foundation walls are damp-proofed on the exterior over parging or concrete. Form-tie holes are sealed first. Masonry gets at least 6 mm of parging and is coved over the footing.
value: Sequence: seal ties → parge (masonry) → damp-proof → drain → backfill
applicable_limits: Damp-proofing is not waterproofing (9.13.3 is used for hydrostatic conditions).

subject: rainscreen wall
claim: Five-year monitoring of five Vancouver rainscreen buildings: ventilated and drained claddings reduce the moisture-damage sensitivity of wood-frame walls. Buoyancy-driven cavity ventilation is usually enough for good drying. Exterior insulation further improves sheathing drying. Site factors strongly change driving-rain load and wind relative to YVR airport data. WUFI 4.1 reproduced field data well.
value: `face_sealed → rainscreen`: reduce sheathing peak wetness and speed drying (qualitative multiplier). Site exposure modifies airport WDR.
source: Finch, G. (2007). *The Performance of Rainscreen Walls in Coastal British Columbia*. MASc thesis, University of Waterloo. See also Finch, G., Hubbs, B. & Dell, D. (2008). Field monitoring of rainscreen walls…, BEST/RCI Building Envelope Symposium 2008 (IIBEC).
applicable_limits: Abstract only. 3–6 storey multi-unit wood-frame buildings. The 2008 PDF was not retrievable (redirect loop).
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: rainscreen cavity
claim: Steady-state analysis of a stucco/panel wall in the coastal BC climate: a 19 mm cavity gives more airflow and drying than 10 mm. Above 19 mm, bigger vents raise airflow but barely change drying. Once ventilation passes a threshold, the sheathing membrane's vapour permeance governs the drying of wet plywood. An optimum ventilation rate exists, and more ventilation can increase wetting if rain leaks in. Cites lab work (Hazleden 2001): top and bottom vents dried faster than bottom-only, and a 19 mm cavity dried faster than 10 mm.
value: `cavity_drying_factor`: 0 mm → 0; 10 mm → ~0.6; 19 mm → 1.0; >19 mm → 1.0 (plateau). The values are illustrative shape; the direction is evidenced.
source: Ge, H. & Ye, Y. (2007). Investigation of Ventilation Drying of Rainscreen Walls in the Coastal Climate of British Columbia. *Thermal Performance of the Exterior Envelopes of Whole Buildings X* (Buildings X), ASHRAE.
applicable_limits: An analysis/simulation paper. The field results were preliminary. Covers panel and stucco walls on 2×6 wood frame.

subject: sheathing drying (seasonal)
claim: In a monitored Vancouver rainscreen wall, sheathing moisture stayed high through winter, began dropping in mid-March, was relatively dry from May to September, and was rising again by October. Driving-rain events were followed by moisture peaks first in the strapping and then in the sheathing.
value: `drying_season = May–Sep` and `wetting_season = Oct–Apr` for Vancouver. WDR event → strapping peak → sheathing peak (lag).
source: Hubbs & Hircock 2003 (as above), Fig. 6a and Fig. 8 discussion
applicable_limits: One cavity on one building in 2002. Uses a relative 0–100 moisture scale.

subject: wall orientation (drying)
claim: One-year monitoring of three wood-frame homes in West Vancouver. North walls had higher moisture content, dried more slowly and stayed wet in places even in a very dry year. South and east walls were drier because of more solar gain. West walls shaded by large trees were nearly as wet as north walls. Construction defects at sills and penetrations overpowered orientation as a moisture cause.
value: `drying_rate_multiplier` (illustrative values): S ≈ E = 1.0; W (unshaded) ≈ 0.9; W (tree-shaded) ≈ N ≈ 0.6. Any detailing defect overrides orientation.
source: Atwal, L. (2015). *A field study on quality of three First Nation homes on the Squamish Urban Reserve of West Vancouver*. MASc thesis (Building Engineering), British Columbia Institute of Technology.
applicable_limits: 3 houses, 1 year. The abstract gives the direction of the effect, not the multipliers.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: wall orientation (drying)
claim: Preliminary Vancouver hygrothermal modelling found hygIRC predicting the highest moisture load on east walls, while WUFI showed negligible orientation differences once cavity ventilation was included. Material data discrepancies were large.
value: In a ventilated rainscreen, orientation effects on the sheathing should be weaker than on the cladding face.
source: Search-index summary of a BCIT / Canada Masonry Design Centre paper; see Unverified.
applicable_limits: Not read directly.

subject: coatings maintenance
claim: BC Housing guidance for residential buildings: review paint annually. Look for patterns of weathering and plan partial repainting of more sun-exposed areas. Seven or more years after the last painting, or on blistering or extreme fading, prepare and repaint. Other sidings may need repainting by year 10. Check the underlying wood every 3–4 years. In south-west BC, storm-exposed faces (south and sides) are likely to need repainting more often.
value: `coating_life_wood ≈ 7 yr` (avg exposure). `coating_life_other ≈ 10 yr`. Storm- or sun-exposed faces get a shorter cycle (e.g. ×0.7, illustrative).
source: BC Housing (Feb 2018). *Maintenance Matters No. 1: Paints, Stains and Coatings*. Building Maintenance Bulletin (with Polygon and CHOA).
applicable_limits: Multi-unit residential. Practitioner guidance, not measured. Text was extracted from the PDF, and parts of the layout were garbled.

subject: cladding maintenance
claim: Cladding bulletin: review cladding condition annually (face-sealed walls are most sensitive). Remove vegetation encroaching on cladding annually. Clean wood, vinyl and stucco with **non-pressurised** water or soapy water at multi-year intervals; the checklist intervals are mostly 2–3 years for cleaning and 5–10 years for renewal items. Pressure washing can damage components and drive water behind cladding. Organic debris raises moisture retention. Masonry is very durable; maintenance is cleaning and occasional repointing.
value: `cleaning_interval ≈ 2–3 yr` resets the surface-growth state. `vegetation_contact` adds a wetting and growth penalty. `pressure_wash` adds an ingress event.
source: BC Housing (Feb 2018). *Maintenance Matters No. 8: Cladding*.
applicable_limits: The checklist table's exact row-to-interval mapping was garbled in text extraction. Verify the per-cladding intervals visually before using them.

subject: timber surface weathering
claim: Bare softwood surfaces exposed vertically and facing south in Wisconsin eroded at about 34 µm/yr (southern pine latewood) to about 101 µm/yr (western redcedar earlywood) over 16 years. Earlywood/latewood differences shrank after about 7 years. Vertical-grain lumber eroded faster than flat-grain plywood.
value: `surface_loss_mm = rate × years`, with rate 0.03–0.10 mm/yr. That gives ≈ 0.2–0.5 mm at 5 years, 0.5–1.5 mm at 15 and 1–3 mm at 30. Use for the untreated timber seat surface (weathering only, no abrasion).
source: Williams, R.S., Knaebe, M.T., Sotos, P.G. & Feist, W.C. (2001). Erosion rates of wood during natural weathering. Part I. Effects of grain angle and surface texture. *Wood and Fiber Science* 33(1).
applicable_limits: Vertical south-facing specimens in a continental climate. Excludes foot or seat abrasion, decay and checking. The rate on horizontal seats may differ (Part III studies exposure angle; not read).
suggestion_reason: no reading marker in file; calculated but not fully read

subject: Vancouver rainfall
claim: Mean annual rainfall is 1,152.8 mm (precipitation 1,189 mm; snowfall 38 cm). Monthly rainfall (mm): Jan 157, Feb 99, Mar 112, Apr 88, May 65, Jun 54, Jul 36, Aug 37, Sep 51, Oct 121, Nov 186, Dec 148. Oct–Mar carries about 72% of the year's rain.
value: Month-indexed `rain_mm[m]` to drive ageing simulations. Wet season Oct–Mar.
source: Environment and Climate Change Canada, *Canadian Climate Normals 1981–2010*, station VANCOUVER INT'L A (1108447), via MSC GeoMet API collection `climate-normals`
applicable_limits: The airport is drier than the city and North Shore: the code value for the city is 1,325 mm (see below). Use as the "low-exposure" baseline.

subject: Vancouver rain days
claim: Days with rainfall per year by threshold: ≥0.2 mm 165.1; ≥5 mm 74.6; ≥10 mm 40.8; ≥25 mm 6.6. Nov: 19.9 / 11.2 / 7.0 / 1.5. Jul: 6.3 / 2.4 / 1.3 / 0.2.
value: Storm generator: P(day ≥ 10 mm) ≈ 0.11 per year-day, 0.23 in Nov. "Heavy storm" = 25 mm/day, about 6–7 times a year.
source: ECCC 1981–2010 normals, as above
applicable_limits: Daily totals; no hourly intensities.

subject: Vancouver rainfall (1991–2020)
claim: 1991–2020 normals for YVR: rainfall 1,119.2 mm/yr on 166.0 rain days (≥0.2 mm). Jan 162 mm, Nov 171 mm, Jul 34 mm. Mean 15:00 RH 70.6%. Sunshine 1,937.5 h.
value: Updated baseline. Differences from 1981–2010 are small (about −3% rain).
source: Wikipedia, "Climate of Vancouver", climate table citing ECCC Canadian Climate Normals 1991–2020
applicable_limits: Secondary transcription. The page's own footnotes mix the 1981–2010 and 1991–2020 periods. Verify against the ECCC CSV before final use.

subject: Vancouver design climate
claim: City of Vancouver design climate (except Granville & 41st): 15-min rain 10 mm; one-day rain (1/50 yr) 112 mm (107 mm at Granville & 41st); annual rain 1,325 mm; annual total precipitation 1,400 mm; moisture index 1.44; driving-rain wind pressure (1/5 yr) 160 Pa; HDD (below 18 °C) 2,925; hourly wind pressure 0.35 kPa (1/10) and 0.45 kPa (1/50).
value: `design_burst = 10 mm in 15 min` (≈ 40 mm/h). `extreme_day = 112 mm`. DRWP 160 Pa gives a wind speed during rain of √(2×160/1.2) ≈ 16 m/s (derived, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³).
source: Vancouver Building By-law 2014, Div. B, Tables 1.1.3.1.A and 1.1.3.1.B (Climatic Data for the City of Vancouver)
applicable_limits: 2014 edition. VBBL 2025 / BCBC 2024 values may differ (01 reports HDD 2825–2925, MI 1.4). The derived wind speed is my calculation.

subject: Vancouver wind
claim: Mean hourly wind speed is 12.2 km/h (≈ 3.4 m/s), ranging from 11.2 km/h (Sep) to 13.2 km/h (Mar). The most frequent direction is **east (90°) in every month**. Per year there are 181 days with at least one hourly speed above 20 km/h, 64 above 30 km/h, 19.4 above 40 km/h and 4.4 above 50 km/h, peaking Nov–Mar.
value: Default storm wind: from E, 5–8 m/s in a typical storm (illustrative mapping from the >20–30 km/h day counts). Gusty days are concentrated in Oct–Mar.
source: ECCC 1981–2010 normals, as above
applicable_limits: All-weather wind, not wind during rain. The airport is open, flat terrain; urban sites are more sheltered.

subject: wind-driven rain direction
claim: RDH: in Vancouver the primary direction of wind-driven rain is **east**. East-elevation gauges recorded 3× the driving rain of south-elevation gauges on two buildings.
value: `wdr_orientation_weight`: E = 1.0, S ≈ 0.33. N and W are not measured (illustrative ≤ 0.33).
source: Hubbs & Hircock 2003 (see 2a)
applicable_limits: Two buildings, 2002. **Conflicts** with BC Housing MM No. 1, which says storms in south-west BC come from the south and sides. Site-specific channeling (Finch 2007) matters.

subject: wind-driven rain direction
claim: BC Housing: in south-west BC the predominant wind-driven rainstorms commonly hit buildings from the south and sides, so those faces may need repainting sooner.
value: Alternative weighting: S and sides high. Keep as a user-selectable scenario until resolved.
source: BC Housing 2018, *Maintenance Matters No. 1* (see 2a)
applicable_limits: Practitioner statement, not data. Covers the region, not Vancouver specifically.

subject: Vancouver humidity
claim: Mean RH at 06:00 is 85.9% (Jan 89.1%, Jul 81.9%). Mean RH at 15:00 is 70.3% (Jan 81.2%, Jul 61.4%). Mean vapour pressure is 0.71 kPa in Dec and 1.51 kPa in Aug. Fog days 17.6 per year, mostly Sep–Feb.
value: `drying_potential[m]` ∝ (1 − RH15[m]/100) × sunshine[m]. Winter drying potential is about 1/4–1/5 of summer (derived).
source: ECCC 1981–2010 normals, as above
applicable_limits: Air values only. Surface conditions differ with orientation and shading.

subject: Vancouver freeze–thaw
claim: Days with min ≤ 0 °C: 40.9 per year (Dec 12.0, Jan 9.8, Feb 9.4, Nov 5.0, Mar 3.7). Days with max ≤ 0 °C: 3.4. Days with min < −2 °C: 20.5. Days with min < −10 °C: 1.6. Freezing-rain days: 0.8. Degree-days below 0 °C: 30.5. Derived: days with an air freeze–thaw cycle (min ≤ 0 and max > 0) ≈ 40.9 − 3.4 = **37.5 per year**, of which about 20 have min below −2 °C.
value: `ft_cycles_per_year ≈ 37` (air). Damage requires the material to be near saturation, so use `ft_damage_events ≈ ft_cycles × P(wet)`. The wall-base splash zone is the most likely place to be wet.
source: ECCC 1981–2010 normals, as above. Derivation is mine.
applicable_limits: Air temperature at 1.5 m. Surface and in-material cycles differ: shaded north bases may cycle more and sunny faces less. Mild cycles near 0 °C may not freeze pore water.

subject: Vancouver temperature
claim: Mean daily temperature is 4.1 °C in Jan and 18.0 °C in Jul/Aug (annual 10.4 °C). Mean daily max is 6.9 °C in Jan and 22.2 °C in Aug. There are 76.5 days per year above 20 °C and 0.3 days above 30 °C.
value: Biological growth window: most months stay above 5 °C on average, so the moss and algae season is effectively year-round when wet (illustrative).
source: ECCC 1981–2010 normals, as above

subject: Vancouver sunshine
claim: Bright sunshine is 1,937.5 h per year. By month: Jan 60, Feb 91, Mar 135, Apr 185, May 223, Jun 227, Jul 290, Aug 277, Sep 213, Oct 121, Nov 60, Dec 56. That is 22% of possible daylight in Nov–Jan and 59–62% in Jul–Aug. 289 days per year have some measurable sunshine.
value: `solar_drying[m]` scaled by sunshine hours. Dec drying ≈ 0.2 × Jul.
source: ECCC 1981–2010 normals, as above
applicable_limits: Horizontal sunshine duration, not irradiance on vertical façades by orientation (see Gaps).

subject: coastal BC climate
claim: Coastal BC is characterised by long wetting periods and short drying periods in the October–March rainy season, with cool temperatures slowing drying.
value: Seasonal state machine: Oct–Mar net wetting, Apr–Sep net drying.
source: Morrison Hershfield / CMHC 1996 as summarised by GreenBuildingAdvisor (Bailes 2022). Consistent with the ECCC monthly data above.
applicable_limits: Qualitative.

subject: bioreceptivity (concept)
claim: Guillitte defined bioreceptivity as a material's aptitude to be colonised by one or more groups of organisms, without necessarily implying biodeterioration. He also called it the totality of material properties that allow establishment, anchorage and development. He separated it from "accessibility", the colonisation potential of the environment. The framing is neutral, not negative.
value: Treat colonisation potential as two separate inputs: environment exposure (wetness, light, spore supply) × material receptivity. Neither alone produces growth.
source: Sanmartín, P., Miller, A.Z., Prieto, B., Viles, H.A. (2021). Revisiting and reanalysing the concept of bioreceptivity 25 years on. *Science of the Total Environment* 770, 145314. doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.145314. Reports Guillitte, O. (1995) "Bioreceptivity: a new concept for building ecology studies", *Sci. Total Environ.* 167, 215–220.
applicable_limits: Conceptual. Most underlying work is lab-based and on stone. Gives no timescales.

subject: bioreceptivity types
claim:
Bioreceptivity types:
- **Primary:** the fresh material as placed.
- **Secondary:** after weathering or the colonisers themselves have changed the surface.
- **Tertiary:** after physical human action such as cleaning or abrasion.
- **Quaternary (proposed):** after added coatings, consolidants or biocides.
Recolonisation after cleaning is reported to be faster than first colonisation. Added treatments can become new habitat or slow drying, which raises bioreceptivity. Guillitte held that secondary bioreceptivity is often the more important in practice.
value: A surface's receptivity rises as it weathers (primary→secondary). After cleaning, regrowth starts from a higher baseline than on the new surface. A newly applied coating resets receptivity to "unknown" and may raise it.
source: Sanmartín et al. 2021 (as ev.eco.01)
applicable_limits: Opinion paper. The "faster recolonisation" point rests on a few cited studies, mainly on stone heritage. No rates given.

subject: material factors in bioreceptivity
claim:
Intrinsic material factors:
- Guillitte & Dreesen (1995, lab, six months) found bioreceptivity controlled mainly by surface roughness, initial porosity and mineralogy.
- For granite, high open porosity, high capillary water content and roughness most promote phototroph colonisation.
- For limestone, roughness is key but there is no consensus beyond that.
- Colour is listed as an intrinsic factor.
value: Rougher, more porous, more water-absorbent surfaces move faster through the stages. Smooth, dense, low-absorption surfaces move slower.
source: Sanmartín et al. 2021, reporting Guillitte & Dreesen (1995); Prieto & Silva (2005); Vázquez-Nion et al. (2018)
applicable_limits: Mainly lab, mostly natural stone. The relative weight of each factor is unresolved for most materials.

subject: colonisation sequence (lab)
claim:
Lab chamber sequence (Guillitte & Dreesen 1995, as summarised):
- Green algae appeared first, on concrete, at about two weeks.
- Algae then appeared on porous limestone, brick and mortar.
- Cyanobacteria and mosses followed on concrete.
- At six months, porous limestone and concrete were heavily colonised. Compact limestone, brick and mortar were barely colonised.
Speed differs between organism groups and between materials.
value: Order of stages: clean → biofilm → algae → (cyanobacterial crust) → moss. Different materials progress at different speeds under the same exposure.
source: Sanmartín et al. 2021, summarising Guillitte, O. & Dreesen, R. (1995), *Sci. Total Environ.* 167, 365–374
applicable_limits: Accelerated: nutrient-rich water was sprinkled with spores supplied. The weeks to months timeline does not transfer to the field. Only six materials were tested.

subject: building-scale factors
claim:
Building-scale factors (cm–m) strongly modify colonisation:
- Surface angle, aspect and position on the building set the water and thermal regime.
- The same stone in different details (e.g. string course vs baluster) behaves differently.
- Runoff from copper elements can limit growth below them.
- Nutrient wash-off from tree canopies can increase it.
- Mortar, salts and solutions alter in-wall porosity.
value: Horizontal and sloped ledges, and surfaces under tree canopy drip, advance faster. Vertical, sheltered or copper-runoff zones advance slower.
source: Sanmartín et al. 2021 (§3.1, §3.4)
applicable_limits: Qualitative argument with examples; the authors call for field studies. The copper point is an example, not a measured effect.

subject: pioneer colonisers (greening)
claim: Phototrophic micro-organisms (algae, cyanobacteria) are pioneer colonisers of inorganic building materials. "Greening" is the first step of sequential colonisation. Early communities on fresh material are dominated by fast-growing, well-dispersed organisms. More competitive organisms replace them later. Pioneer algal films are sometimes negligible to stone integrity, or even protective.
value: The first visible stage on any wet mineral surface is a green or dark film. Later stages replace rather than simply add to it. Early film = appearance change, not damage.
applicable_limits: Heritage stone focus. The protective vs damaging role of each stage is debated.

subject: biological growth on masonry
claim:
Historic England research summary:
- Moss indicates and sustains high moisture, which can damage masonry. Some lichens and bacteria actively cause deterioration.
- Algae supply nutrients for later growth and cause disfiguring discolouration.
- Changes in temperature and in rainfall frequency and intensity are linked to more observed "greening".
- Water cleaning removes some surface. High-pressure cleaning roughens it.
- In trials, some biocides stopped working after about three months.
- Stone properties and surface orientation (horizontal vs vertical) affected biocide effectiveness and the rate of recolonisation.
value: Moss stage = persistent wet microclimate at that spot. Each aggressive cleaning roughens the surface and raises later receptivity. Chemical treatment holds a surface "clean" only briefly.
source: Stewart, J. & Willett, C. (2019). Control of Biological Growth on Masonry. *Historic England Research* Issue 12, published 29 May 2019.
applicable_limits: Historic porous stone and brick. Small-scale trials on two limestones. The ~3-month biocide figure is an early trial result.

subject: algae on render facades
claim:
Trade-press summary of German research:
- Algae and fungi appear mostly on north- and west-facing facades, especially with trees nearby, because they get little sun and dry slowly.
- Growth is mainly in spring and autumn (damp, not too cold).
- Wind brings nutrients.
- The problem also affects concrete, fibre-cement and metal cladding.
- Biocides in renders must be water-soluble, so they leach out.
- In a Fraunhofer weathering test, none of 33 render/paint/biocide combinations protected for more than five years.
value: North- and west-facing and tree-shaded faces advance one stage faster than sunny faces. "Biocidal" finishes delay the algae stage by only a few years.
source: DETAIL (2013, 1 Feb). Research and practice: Algae growth on ETICS – a problem without a solution? DETAIL magazine (no author listed).
applicable_limits: Mainly insulated render systems (ETICS). Northern-hemisphere orientation. Vancouver's wet maritime winter differs from central Europe's seasonality. The Fraunhofer test was not seen directly.

subject: render facade surface moisture
claim: Biological growth on insulated render facades is linked to high surface moisture, which comes mainly from external condensation and wind-driven rain. Slow drying keeps the surface wet longer and raises the risk. A one-year monitoring study of a building with four cardinal facades quantified how orientation affects wetting.
value: Wetting sources: rain exposure + night condensation. Drying sources: sun + air movement. The tool's "wet-hours" proxy should combine both, by orientation.
source: Barreira, E. & de Freitas, V.P. (2013). Experimental study of the hygrothermal behaviour of External Thermal Insulation Composite Systems (ETICS). *Building and Environment*. doi:10.1016/j.buildenv.2013.02.001
applicable_limits: Insulated render only. Mild Atlantic climate. The orientation-by-orientation results were not read (abstract only).
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: cementitious materials colonisation
claim:
Cement-based materials:
- **Lab:** In accelerated algal-fouling tests, a lower-pH magnesium-phosphate binder fouled faster than ordinary Portland cement, and fouling rate was governed by roughness and porosity.
- **Field:** In outdoor exposure at three sites (Barcelona, Montseny, Ghent; two inclinations), the specimens showed **no visible colonisation** during the study. The authors concluded that environment mattered more than material properties at that stage. Ordinary Portland cement specimens carried more microbial colonisation than the lab favourite. Optimised composition alone is not enough for rapid growth.
value: In the first years, exposure (wetness) outweighs mix design. A "bioreceptive" mix alone does not make a surface green quickly.
source: Manso, S., Calvo-Torras, M.Á., De Belie, N., Segura, I., Aguado, A. (2015). Evaluation of natural colonisation of cementitious materials: effect of bioreceptivity and environmental conditions. *Science of the Total Environment* 512–513, 444–453. doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2015.01.086. Also: Manso, S. et al. (2014). Bioreceptivity evaluation of cementitious materials designed to stimulate biological growth. *Sci. Total Environ.* 481, 232–241.
applicable_limits: Mediterranean and NW-European sites. The exposure duration was not found in the abstract (see Gaps). Small specimens, not building walls.

subject: bioreceptive concrete mix
claim:
Concrete mix tests:
- Three measures significantly increased bioreceptivity: lightweight crushed expanded-clay aggregate, a bone-ash addition, and a surface retarder (rougher exposed surface).
- A higher water–cement ratio did not.
- The authors found that pH below 10 was not necessary for growth, against a common assumption.
value: Exposed-aggregate or retarded (rough) concrete advances faster. Do not assume that fresh cement alkalinity reliably delays the algae stage.
source: Veeger, M., Ottelé, M., Prieto, A. (2021). Making bioreceptive concrete: formulation and testing of bioreceptive concrete mixtures. *Journal of Building Engineering* 44, 102545. doi:10.1016/j.jobe.2021.102545
applicable_limits: Lab, inoculated. Volume number and abstract wording seen only in search excerpts.

subject: hemp-lime mould
claim:
Contrary evidence on hemp-lime alkalinity:
- Lime-bound hemp-lime showed no microbial growth at 75% relative humidity. The critical level lies between 75% and 85%.
- Bare hemp shiv has low resistance, similar to wood. Lime protects it.
value: Hemp-lime at the base: treat as mould-resistant only while it stays relatively dry. Persistent splash or wet ground at the foot removes that protection.
source: Johansson, S., Balksten, K., Strandberg-de Bruijn, P.B. (2022). Risk for mould growth on hemp-lime at different relative humidity. *Construction Technologies and Architecture* 1, 588–594. doi:10.4028/www.scientific.net/CTA.1.588
applicable_limits: Lab, constant humidity at 15 and 23 °C. Interior mould risk, not exterior colonisation by algae or moss. No field data.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: concrete panel geometry
claim: Six concrete facade panels with different surface geometries (slag cement, w/c 0.6, uncured, so highly porous) were moss-inoculated and kept in a greenhouse for four months. The panel with the most prominent relief was colonised most. The plain panel was colonised least, despite high water absorption. Geometry played a substantial role.
value: Relief (grooves, pockets, ledges) is a stronger lever than porosity alone. A plain flat face advances slowest.
source: Mustafa, K.F., Prieto, A., Ottelé, M. (2021). The role of geometry on a self-sustaining bio-receptive concrete panel for facade application. *Sustainability* 13(13), 7453.
applicable_limits: Inoculated, ideal greenhouse conditions, four months, qualitative observation. Not a field result.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: bioreceptive panels (outdoor)
claim:
UCL Bartlett "Computational Seeding of Bio-Receptive Materials":
- Eighteen bioreceptive concrete panels were exposed outdoors in an urban setting for 335 days, with algae and moss growth monitored.
- Panels with more horizontal or diagonal geometry and more surface area retained more water.
- A vertical "curtain" geometry shed the most water.
- Growth differed clearly by geometry.
- The aim is to avoid the irrigation and maintenance costs of conventional green walls.
value: Bioreceptive panels at the base: growth stage advances with water-holding geometry. Vertical fluting sheds water and slows growth.
source: UCL Bartlett (2024, Jul). Computational Seeding of Bio-Receptive Materials (research project page; PI M. Cruz). Background: Cruz, M. & Beckett, R. (2016). Bioreceptive design: a novel approach to biodigital materiality. *arq: Architectural Research Quarterly* 20(1), 51–64. doi:10.1017/S1359135516000130
applicable_limits: Project summary; no coverage figures published on the page. The full 2016 paper text was not read (only the publisher record). Seeded panels, so not natural colonisation.

subject: lichen colonisation lag
claim:
Lichen colonisation of newly exposed stone has a lag:
- **Gravestones:** establishment is erratic, with a minimum exposure period before colonisation. Estimates from dated gravestones and comparable surfaces range from about 5 to 18 years.
- **Slate:** colonisation of new slate was greater where small cracks were present.
- Some long-lived crust lichens are not first colonisers. They replace earlier, faster-growing ones.
value: The lichen stage should not appear on new mineral surfaces in the first few years. It typically enters in the 5–15-year window and is patchy and erratic. Cracks and joints are colonised first.
source: Armstrong, R.A. Lichenometric dating (lichenometry) and the biology of the lichen genus *Rhizocarpon*: challenges and future directions (invited review, accepted manuscript, Aston University repository). Cites Innes (1983), Evans & Archer (1999), Winchester & Chaujer (2002).
applicable_limits: Upland and cool-temperate sites, mainly siliceous stone and one crust-lichen group. Not urban, not cementitious. Journal and year of the review not confirmed (see Unverified).

subject: recolonisation after cleaning
claim: A review of recolonisation after cleaning stone heritage found few studies, with differing treatments, substrates and climates. Fungi appear to recolonise faster than other groups. Short-term studies detect only generalist recolonisers. Long-term studies show specialists returning, similar to the community that was removed.
value: After cleaning, the surface returns first to a generic film. Over longer horizons it trends back toward its previous stage mix.
source: Prieto Lamas, B., Paz Bermúdez, G., López de Silanes, M.E., Montojo Santos, C., Pérez Velón, D. (2024). Current knowledge regarding biological recolonization of stone cultural heritage after cleaning treatments. *Journal of Building Engineering* 87, 109091. doi:10.1016/j.jobe.2024.109091
applicable_limits: Stone heritage only. The authors say firm conclusions are not possible. No rates.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: climbing plants (ivy)
claim:
Historic England guidance on climbing plants on walls:
- **Benefits:** a cover moderates temperature extremes and wetting–drying cycles and traps pollutants and salts.
- **Attachment:** aerial attachment roots are superficial and do not take moisture from the wall.
- **"Proper" roots** form where the base is cut, the wall is very damp, or organic matter such as leaf litter accumulates. They exploit existing cracks and enlarge them.
- **Problems:** the plant can block gutters and downpipes, conceal damp and hinder inspection.
value: A climber at the base: protective on sound wall faces. Escalates to damage only where it roots into existing cracks, damp spots or debris-filled joints. It also hides the condition beneath.
source: Historic England (updated 8 Aug 2024). Ivy on Walls. Technical guidance. Underlying research: Coombes, M., Viles, H., Cathersides, A., Ivy on Walls research report (Historic England Research Report 30/2017).
applicable_limits: Historic masonry; one climber type. The research report itself was not read.

subject: wear from contact (climbing)
claim:
Experimental repeated climbing:
- On a never-climbed sandstone boulder, 500 ascents reduced lichen cover by about 4–10%, concentrated at footholds and combined foot/hand holds. Most of the loss came during the first ascents.
- A follow-up on limestone, granite and sandstone (500 ascents each) reported losses up to about 15% at holds. Sandstone was most vulnerable. Sandstone cover had only partly recovered after three years.
value: Touched and stepped zones (seat edges, step nosings, handholds) stay one or more stages "younger" than adjacent untouched surface. The first months of use do most of the clearing. Regrowth after use stops is slow.
source: Schweizer, A.-M., Höschler, L., Steinbauer, M.J. (2021). The physical damage of climbing activity on sandstone lichen cover. *Sustainability* 13(24), 13590. doi:10.3390/su132413590. And: Österle, I.A., Paulus, S., Schwietering, A., Audorff, V., Steinbauer, M.J. (2025). Mechanical impacts of climbing on cliff vegetation: contrasting management concepts. *People and Nature*. doi:10.1002/pan3.70207 (per University of Bayreuth press release 114/2025, 17 Dec 2025).
applicable_limits: Natural rock, not building materials. Climbing contact is more abrasive than sitting. Proxy for wear only.

subject: timber moisture / decay
claim:
Canadian Wood Council:
- Wood at or below 19% moisture content counts as dry.
- Decay typically needs about 30% or more for an extended period.
- Most fungi grow fastest at about 15–25 °C and grow very slowly or not at all near freezing.
- Mould can start above about 80% relative humidity.
- Rain, snow, ground contact and moisture traps where wood meets other materials are the key sources. Wood separated from the ground by concrete can still collect moisture unless detailed to drain.
- Horizontal members dry more slowly than vertical ones.
- Outdoors, use treated or naturally durable wood, keep it away from water sources, and detail it to re-dry.
value: Timber at the base reaches the decay stage only where it stays wet for long periods: ground contact, splash, moisture traps, horizontal upper faces. Vertical, ventilated, re-drying timber stays at the "weathered" stage.
source: Canadian Wood Council (2004). Managing Moisture and Wood. Building Performance Series No. 6 (with Forintek Canada Corp.).
applicable_limits: Focus on storage and construction moisture. Thresholds are rules of thumb, not species-specific.

subject: wood decay conditions
claim:
NRC digest on decay:
- **Five conditions** are required: inoculum, wood, moisture, oxygen and suitable temperature. Removing any one usually prevents decay.
- **Moisture:** wood is not immune until below about 20% moisture content. Decay fungi thrive at about 35–50%. Once established, decay can raise moisture content itself.
- **Oxygen:** saturated or submerged wood does not decay.
- **Temperature:** decay is faster in summer than in winter.
- **Ground contact:** soil carries decay fungi into wood touching it.
- **Speed:** extensive rot has occurred within two or three years in some cases.
value: Decay stage triggers: timber + sustained wetting + ground or soil contact. Once started it accelerates. Fully dry and fully saturated timber both resist decay.
source: Baker, M.C. (1969). Decay of Wood. *Canadian Building Digest* CBD-111. National Research Council Canada, Division of Building Research.
applicable_limits: 1969; general principles, still cited. Temperatures given in °F in the original.

subject: cladding clearance (splash)
claim: National Building Code (Canada) Sentence 9.27.2.4.(1) requires clearance between finished ground and moisture-sensitive cladding. Its stated intent is to limit the chance that rain or meltwater splashes, soaks or pools against the lower cladding, which would cause early deterioration. Product evaluations cite a minimum of 200 mm in NBC 2015.
value: Cladding within the splash band above finished ground (or above mulch or soil raised against it) gets "splash zone" wetting. It advances faster in both the growth and decay stages.
source: NRC Canada, Intent statement for NBC Sentence 9.27.2.4.(1) (archived, NBC 2005 edition). 200 mm figure: CCMC evaluation report 14366-R (Nichiha), citing NBC 2015.
region: Canada (Vancouver uses its own Building By-law based on the national code)
applicable_limits: The intent text is from an archived edition. The 200 mm value was seen only in search excerpts of a product evaluation. Confirm the current Vancouver By-law wording.

subject: carpenter ants
claim:
BC Government carpenter ant guidance:
- Nests are in moist, decaying wood: rotting stumps, logs, woodpiles and rotting wood in houses. Some nest in drier wall voids.
- Entry routes include vegetation touching the house, lower siding edges, fences joined to the house, and crawl-space vents.
- Prevention: keep wood siding and structures out of contact with soil, remove rotted stumps and landscape wood, store firewood raised and away, prune plants off the walls, fix moisture-damaged wood.
- The ants tunnel; they do not eat wood.
value: Edge features that raise insect pressure on a timber base: rotting landscape timber, wood-soil contact, plants touching the wall, damp decaying wood. Removing them lowers it.
source: Province of British Columbia (last updated 5 Aug 2020). Managing Carpenter Ant Pests.
applicable_limits: Homeowner guidance; no data on infestation rates.

subject: carpenter ants
claim:
Two extension sources, partly in conflict:
- **Penn State:** carpenter ants usually do not infest sound wood below about 15% moisture content. Nest expansion into timbers rarely causes structural damage. Parent colonies are often outdoors in trees, logs or waste wood and send satellites indoors.
- **Pacific Northwest Insect Management Handbook:** carpenter ants can nest in sound, dry wood, wall voids and foam insulation. Outdoor parent colonies feed indoor satellites. Homes near forest see more activity.
value: Insect risk at the base is primarily a moisture/decay co-factor: it rises with the decay stage. A residual low risk exists even for dry timber near woodland edges.
source: Jacobs, S. (2002, rev. 2014). Carpenter Ants. Penn State Extension. Pacific Northwest Insect Management Handbook, "Wood-infesting pests – Ant" (Oregon State Univ., Washington State Univ., Univ. of Idaho).
applicable_limits: The two sources disagree on dry-wood nesting. The PNW handbook is the more regionally relevant. No quantified damage timelines.

subject: mulch / gravel at wall foot
claim:
University of Kentucky termite guidance:
- Keep wood siding and frames at least six inches above ground.
- Keep soil next to the foundation from staying consistently moist (gutters, grading, irrigation).
- Avoid dense plantings and vines touching the house.
- Mulch attracts termites mainly through retained moisture. Crushed stone or pea gravel are comparable because they also keep the underlying soil moist. Use mulch sparingly and never against siding or frames.
value: Any mulch or gravel layer against the wall keeps the soil beneath it moist, so it raises base wetness. A bare gap at the wall foot lowers it. Gravel is not automatically "dry".
source: Potter, M.F. Protecting Your Home Against Termites. Entfact-605, University of Kentucky Department of Entomology.
applicable_limits: Written for subterranean termites in a warm, humid US climate. The moisture logic transfers; the termite pressure does not (see Unverified on BC termites). No measured soil moisture data.

subject: tree roots in drains
claim:
Tree roots and sewers:
- Interference is most likely in old systems and cracked pipes.
- Risk is higher with jointed, shallow and small-diameter pipes and fast-growing trees.
- Roots are reported to cause over half of sewer blockages.
- Small pipes often need root clearing every one to two years.
value: Roots enter drains at the base mainly where joints or cracks already exist. Risk rises with drain age and shallowness, and with vigorous woody planting nearby.
source: Randrup, T.B., McPherson, E.G., Costello, L.R. (2001). Tree root intrusion in sewer systems: review of extent and costs. *Journal of Infrastructure Systems* 7(1), 26–31. doi:10.1061/(ASCE)1076-0342(2001)7:1(26)
applicable_limits: Municipal sewers, not perforated foundation drains or gravel strips. Statistics are reported values.
suggestion_reason: abstract read; primary source with url

subject: trees near foundations (clay)
claim:
NHBC Standards Chapter 4.2:
- Trees, hedgerows and shrubs take moisture from the ground. In cohesive (shrinkable) soils such as clay, this causes significant volume change and ground movement.
- Foundations must either accommodate the movement or go deep enough that damaging movement is unlikely.
- Required depth depends on: the soil's plasticity index; the distance from the trunk centre to the foundation face; and the tree's mature height and water demand.
- Root barriers are not an acceptable alternative.
- Removing trees can cause heave.
value: Wall-foot planting risk is soil-dependent: on shrinkable clay, risk scales with plant size and water demand ÷ distance. On non-shrinkable soils, the indirect (shrinkage) risk is low.
source: NHBC (2026 ed.). NHBC Standards, Chapter 4.2 "Building near trees". National House-Building Council, UK.
applicable_limits: Full text is behind a login. Clauses were seen only as search excerpts of the official pages. UK soils and climate. Does not give Vancouver soil classes.

subject: tree setbacks on marine clay
claim:
City of Ottawa, sensitive marine clay soils:
- **2005 policy:** street trees had to be low water demand and set back from foundations by their full mature height.
- **2017 guidelines:** for street trees, the setback may drop to 4.5 m for small (mature height ≤7.5 m) and medium (7.5–14 m) trees, only if conditions are met. These include low/medium plasticity soils (modified plasticity index generally ≤40%), a minimum rooting soil volume (25 m³ small, 30 m³ medium, to 1.5 m depth) and engineering confirmation.
- Large trees still need the full mature height.
- The review drew on NHBC 4.2.
value: Canadian precedent for a soil-conditional setback: on clay, keep trees about their mature height from the wall unless engineered. Smaller trees can sit closer only with adequate rooting volume.
source: City of Ottawa (2017). Tree Planting in Sensitive Marine Clay Soils – 2017 Guidelines.
applicable_limits: Specific to Champlain Sea marine clays. Not applicable to most Vancouver soils without a geotechnical check. Covers street trees in new subdivisions.

subject: rain gardens
claim:
City of North Vancouver residential stormwater tool sheet:
- Rain gardens (shallow planted infiltration areas) should be at least 3 m from the house to keep water away from the foundation.
- They should have a perforated underdrain and an overflow connected to the storm system.
- Specified soil mix is mostly sand with some fines and organics, 450 mm deep.
value: Do not place infiltrating planting beds directly at the wall foot. Within about 3 m, a planted strip should drain and not pond. Ponding beds near the wall raise base wetness.
source: City of North Vancouver. Stormwater Management Tools for Residential Development – Tool 5: Rain Gardens (tool sheet, c. 2017).
applicable_limits: Infiltration features, not ordinary planting. Assumes footing drains. Date taken from file metadata.

subject: hemp concrete fungal growth
claim:
Hemp concretes:
- Fresh material can carry substantial fungal populations despite binder alkalinity.
- After 18 months of static and dynamic ageing, no fungal growth was observed. The authors attribute this to drying and mineralisation of the plant aggregate.
- A separate accelerated-ageing study reported mould at very high humidity once carbonation had lowered binder pH.
value: Lime-based bio-aggregate wall bases: the alkalinity benefit fades as the surface carbonates. Keep them out of the persistent wet band.
source: Delannoy, G. et al. Impacts of alkalinity and environmental ageing on fungal growth in hemp concretes. RILEM TC 253-MCI conference, Toulouse, June 2018 (HAL hal-03618345). Marceau, S. et al.
